title: Aad sach: the meaning
hookLine: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and true hereafter, says Nanak

lines: TRUE: IT HAPPENS TO BE SO.
cards: We use the word true in two ways. A true statement happens to be so: it's raining, it's Tuesday. That kind of true can change by tomorrow.
A true friend is the one who stays, who still shows up after the move, the divorce, the bad year. That kind of true is about lasting. Guru Nanak's salok uses the second kind.
Yesterday you heard it; today, what it says.

teach.b: Sach is truth, the true. In Gurbani it's more than a correct fact. It's a name for the One: the reality that doesn't wear out.
The Mool Mantar said it first: sat naam, truth is the name. Now the salok spells it out in four steps.
Following Macauliffe, in plain words: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true even now, and, says Nanak, true it shall be hereafter. Aad: the beginning, before anything was.
Jugaad: through the ages, the long cycles of time Indian thought counts in. Hai bhee: is, even now, at this moment. Hosee bhee: will be, ever after.
Listen for the small word bhee: also, even. True then, and also now. True now, and also later.
The passing of time takes nothing away. Notice what isn't there: no argument, no proof. Guru Nanak doesn't reason his way to it; he states it, the way you'd name a mountain you can see.
Japji will spend thirty-eight pauris on how a person comes to live inside that truth. And notice the name in the middle: Nanak.
The Guru signs his hymns with it, and the later Gurus in the Granth sign theirs as Nanak too.

It's a signature, and a witness: this is what Nanak saw. Why begin here? Because everything that follows, a restless mind, a changing world, fame and loss, stands in front of something that doesn't change.
That's the ground Japji is built on.

how: Sikhs recite the salok on the eternal truth every morning after the Mool Mantar, and sach, the True, is a name for God found all through the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: the true that lasts, a name for the One
a vow or promise made before the sangat
a correct fact that could change by tomorrow

games.q: match the words to their meaning.

s: in Gurbani, sach only means a correct fact
it's a name for the One, the reality that doesn't wear out.
the salok argues its way to its claim
there's no argument; Guru Nanak states it, like naming a mountain.
later Gurus also sign their hymns as Nanak
the name is a signature and a witness.

games.q: the salok names four times. which of these is not one of them?
games.why: beginning, ages, now, hereafter: the verse doesn't need a personal date; it covers all time.

practice: Picture yourself at seven, at fifteen, a year ago, and now: your face, your work, your opinions, your address have all changed.
Look for one thing that hasn't, maybe a way you love people, a stubborn honesty, a sense of wonder, a fear you've always faced anyway, and name it quietly to yourself: true then, and true now.
If you pray, you can hold it up to the One the salok calls true.

wordCard.voice: Sach. Truth, the true that lasts: true in the beginning, through the ages, now, and hereafter.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sach, truth, the True. the small mark under the last letter is mostly silent.

carryVoice: Your line: true then, true now. Four times named, and nothing taken away. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (salok after the Mool Mantar)
Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji (opening salok)
